pll1d38c1-d1e3501.summary: Returns to the topic: foreknowledge is of future things only, but of all, good and evil; knowledge or wisdom is of past, present, and future, temporal and eternal, since God knows himself.
claims: Foreknowledge concerns all future things.
God's knowledge extends to himself and all things.

pll1d38c1-d1e3506.summary: Raises the question whether God's knowledge or foreknowledge causes things, or things cause his knowledge.

pll1d38c1-d1e3510.summary: Argues that foreknowledge seems to cause what it foreknows and give it necessity: nothing would be future unless foreknown, and what is foreknown cannot fail to happen without God's foreknowledge being deceived, which is impossible. The same holds for knowledge.

pll1d38c1-d1e3513.summary: Cites De Trinitate XV in support: God knew all temporal things without beginning; creatures are not known because they are, but are because he knows them; he created because he knew, and knew created things as he knew them to be created, nothing being added to his wisdom.
claims: Things are because God knows them, not the reverse.
God's knowledge receives nothing from creatures.

pll1d38c1-d1e3547.summary: Cites De Trinitate VI similarly: times pass but nothing passes from God's knowledge; created things are not known because made but made because unchangeably known. So God's knowledge seems the cause of what it knows.
claims: Things are made because God knows them.

pll1d38c1-d1e3561.summary: Objects: then God's knowledge would cause all evils, since he knows them, making God author of evil, which is false. So God's knowledge is not cause of all it knows.
claims: God is not author of evil.
God's knowledge is not the cause of all it knows.

pll1d38c1-d1e3573.summary: Denies also that future things cause God's foreknowledge: though they would not be future unless foreknown, they are not foreknown because future; otherwise something alien would cause the eternal and the Creator's foreknowledge would depend on creatures.
claims: Future things do not cause God's foreknowledge.
The Creator's knowledge does not depend on creatures.

pll1d38c1-d1e3585.summary: Cites Origen on Romans: something will not be because God knows it will be, but because it will be, God knows it before it happens.
claims: Origen says things are foreknown because they will be.

pll1d38c1-d1e3604.summary: Notes that this seems to contradict Augustine: Origen makes future things causes of foreknowledge, Augustine foreknowledge the cause of things.

pll1d38c1-d1e3610.summary: Resolves: future things are in no way causes of God's knowledge. Origen means only that what is future is known before it happens and would not be known unless future, a cause 'without which not.' Likewise God's knowledge, as mere knowing, is a cause only without which things would not be; but if 'knowledge' includes good pleasure and disposition, it rightly causes what God does, since God's knowledge is taken as knowing alone or as knowing with good pleasure.
claims: Future things are not causes of God's knowledge.
Origen indicates only a condition, not a cause.
Knowledge with good pleasure and disposition causes what God does.

pll1d38c1-d1e3626.summary: Reads Augustine accordingly: 'they are because he knew' means because it pleased the knower and he disposed them. Augustine speaks of goods, creatures God makes, which he knows by good pleasure and disposition as well as knowledge.
claims: Augustine's 'because he knew' includes good pleasure and disposition.
Augustine speaks of goods God makes.

pll1d38c1-d1e3635.summary: Evils God knows and foreknows by knowledge alone, not good pleasure. He foreknows and foretells what he will not do, as the Jews' unbelief, which he did not cause or compel; nor would he have foreknown it unless they would have it.
claims: God foreknows evils without causing them.
Foreknowledge of sin does not compel the sinner.

pll1d38c1-d1e3638.summary: Cites Augustine on John: God foretold the Jews' unbelief but did not make it; he compels no one to sin because he foreknew sins, which were theirs, not his. Since his foreknowledge cannot err, those he foreknew would sin are the ones who sin; had they willed good, they would have been foreseen doing good.
claims: God foreknows sins that are the sinners', not his own.
Foreknowledge does not compel sin.
Had people willed good, God would have foreseen that.

pll1d38c1-d1e3656.summary: Concludes that God's foreknowledge does not cause the evils foreknown, since he foreknows them not as maker nor as his but as others'; he foreknows them by knowledge alone, not by the good pleasure of authority. Conversely he foreknows goods as his own, as what he will do, with knowledge and the good pleasure of authority together.
claims: God foreknows evils as others', by knowledge alone.
God foreknows goods as his own, with good pleasure.

pl-l1d38c1.summary: Asks whether God's knowledge or foreknowledge is the cause of things or things the cause of his knowledge. It seems foreknowledge causes things and imposes necessity, since what is foreknown cannot fail to happen, and Augustine says things are because God knows them, not the reverse. But then God would cause evils, which is false; and things cannot cause God's foreknowledge, or the eternal would depend on creatures. Origen says things are foreknown because they will be. Lombard reconciles them: future things are not causes of God's knowledge, Origen meaning only that without them they would not be known; God's knowledge as mere knowing is a cause only as a condition without which they would not be, but knowledge including good pleasure and disposition is the cause of what God does. Augustine speaks of goods God makes. Evils God foreknows by knowledge alone, not good pleasure: he foreknew the Jews' unbelief but did not cause it, foreknowing their sins, not his own.
claims: God's foreknowledge does not of itself cause things or impose necessity.
If foreknowledge caused all things, God would cause evils, which is false.
Future things are not causes of God's foreknowledge; the eternal does not depend on creatures.
Origen means only that things would not be foreknown unless they were to be.
Knowledge as mere knowing is a cause only 'without which not'; knowledge with good pleasure and disposition causes what God does.
God foreknows evils by knowledge alone, not good pleasure.
God foreknew sinners' sins as theirs, not his, and did not compel them.
